The order of the items has been modified to group similar items (see http://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/spirit-2013-statement-defining-standard-protocol-items-for-clinical-trials/ ). Background Background and rationale {6a} Spinal cord damage disrupts nerve connections between the brain and the body’s ascending sensory and descending motor pathways. The spinal cord, part of the central nervous system, transports nerve signals in and out of the brain and cooperates with peripheral nerves to enable voluntary and involuntary motor activity, sensory perception, and environmental interaction. The nerve connection is incomplete or completely disrupted when a spinal cord injury occurs. In the former, sub-lesional sensations and movements persist, whereas in the latter all function is lost and paralysis develops [ ]. The phases of spinal cord injury are divided into five phases as follows: (1) Early acute phase (first 2 to 48 h), (2) acute phase (first 2 h to 2 weeks), (3) subacute phase (day 2 to end of the week 2), (4) intermediate phase (week 2 to month 6), and (5) chronic phase (month 6 to onwards) [ ]. Globally, 20·6 million individuals experienced SCI in 2019. The incidence and prevalence of spinal injuries in China have increased by 98.20%, respectively, the most significant increase among G20 countries [ ]. Most traumatic SCIs in 1999 were caused by falls (52.4%). At 26.4%, traffic accidents were the second most common cause. Traffic accidents cause the most SCIs, followed by falls [ ]. SCI can be classified as a complete or incomplete injury based on severity. Incomplete SCI can present as central core syndrome, Brown-Séquard syndrome, anterior cord syndrome, or posterior core syndrome [ ]. Based on the International Standards for Neurological Classification and the American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS), spinal cord injuries are categorized as either complete or incomplete. Complete injuries are classified as AIS-A, whereas incomplete injuries are classified as AIS-B, AIS-C, AIS-D, or AIS-E, depending on the extent of motor and sensory impairment. A person’s injury is considered complete if they lack voluntary anal contraction, which is indicative of a motor lesion in the S4/5 region, as well as sensation surrounding the anus, which is indicative of a sensory lesion in the S4/5 region [ ]. Paralysis is the primary and evident outcome of spinal cord injury (SCI), resulting in patients experiencing either partial or complete lack of sensation and movement [ ]. Human gait requires lower extremity muscle force, joint proprioception, visual balance, and cognition. Joint proprioception and visual function can also impact balance ability. Following a spinal cord injury (SCI), individuals encounter a range of proprioceptive deficits. It is crucial for rehabilitating movement and acquiring new abilities after spinal cord injury (SCI) [ ]. ASIA/IMSOP, the international standard for spinal cord trauma neurological assessment, is the most accurate and closest to standardization. The WISCI improves walking levels more accurately than the FIM, although the FIM measures patient self-care and independence better [ ]. SCI-related changes in muscle function are often examined via electromyography (EMG). Paralyzed muscles exhibit aberrant neuromuscular transmission, motor unit recruitment and discharge patterns, loss of functioning motor units, and structural reorganization, according to electromyography (EMG) analysis [ ]. Clinical outcomes with neurorehabilitation robots are promising. Robot-assisted gait training improves neuroplasticity, which helps injured nerves recover through repetitive training and stimulation. Second, this training can increase a patient’s muscle strength, stability, walking efficiency, and safety [ ]. Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a noninvasive neuromodulation method. This technology may help us understand spinal interneuronal activity and improve rehabilitation for neurological illnesses, including spinal cord injury [ ]. The gold standard for SCI rehabilitation is repetitive motor activity, commonly employed in clinics to help patients recover. Exercise after SCI appears to excite the neural system enough to activate undamaged spinal pathways and residual supraspinal inputs [ ]. The combination of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) with robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) is an area of growing interest. Some research suggests that including tSCS may improve the effects of robotic training on balance and movement; however, specific investigations on this combination in SCI patients are still limited [ , ]. Most existing research has focused on the efficacy of tSCS or RAGT alone, leaving a gap in understanding the potential synergistic effects of these therapies when used together. There is also a lack of reliable biomarkers for functional recovery, with intramuscular electromyography (iEMG) showing promise in other neurological conditions but underexplored in SCI patients undergoing tSCS and RAGT. Although there has been much research on RAGT, this study makes a unique contribution by looking at the combined impacts of RAGT and tSCS. Compared to conventional methodologies, this approach offers new insights into the effectiveness of robotic training by isolating its impact on gait progress. Our findings may greatly aid our understanding of how combining tSCS and RAGT may improve rehabilitation outcomes may be significantly aided by our findings. Furthermore, our research aligns with existing clinical procedures, which frequently combine gait therapy with tSCS. As a biomarker, intramuscular EMG could provide valuable insights into neuromuscular changes during and after rehabilitation, helping tailor rehabilitation programs to individual needs and track progress more accurately. Standardization and protocol development can improve consistency and comparability of future studies, facilitating the development of evidence-based guidelines for clinical practice. Studying the long-term effects of combined tSCS and RAGT can provide evidence of the sustainability of functional improvements, which is crucial for clinical decision-making. Understanding these therapies’ mechanisms can lead to optimized treatment strategies and potentially uncover new therapeutic targets. Objectives {7} This study aimed to determine the effects of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation combined with robot-assisted gait training for improving balance and mobility in patients with incomplete spinal cord injury (intermediate phase). Consequently, the research questions of this investigation are as follows: What are the impacts of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation combined with robot-assisted gait training for improving balance and mobility in patients with spinal cord injury? We hypothesized that (1) combined training will result in more significant changes leading to more substantial enhancements in the functional capacity of balance and mobility in people with SCI. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to (1) examine the effects of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation combined with robot-assisted gait training for improving balance and mobility in people with SCI and (2) provide evidence to clarify the mechanisms by which balance and mobility function recover in people with SCI. Trial design {8} This is a prospective, double-blind, parallel-armed randomized controlled trial. The 20 selected subjects with SCI were divided into two groups: A and B. Group A comprised 13 subjects, and Group B comprised 7 subjects. Group A (the experimental group) received robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) + transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), and Group B (the control group) received conventional physical therapy (CPT) + transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) for 8 weeks, 5 sessions a week. Figure shows the flow chart of the trial process. The checklist of Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) is provided in Additional File 1: Table S1. Methods Study setting {9} The study setting was Xi'an International Medical Center Hospital. Eligibility criteria {10} The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Both male and female subjects who were diagnosed with incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI) and (2) who were rated with an AIS score of B, C, or D on the American Spinal Cord Injury Association Impairment Scale (ASIA scale). (3) Eligible participants must be between 18 and 80 and (4) at least 3 months post-injury (intermediate phase, week 2 to month 6). The exclusion criteria for the study included the following: (1) Having a cardiac pacemaker, (2) having unstable angina or other decompensated heart disease, (3) having a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or dysreflexia of the autonomic system; (4) individuals with a tracheostomy, (5) significant deformity, or stiffness in the hip joint, knee (20° or more of flexion), or ankle (10° or more of plantar flexion) and those with a restricted range of motion are excluded; (6) additional exclusions apply to those lacking cardiovascular conditioning or disabling fatigue; (7) a body weight greater than 135 kg, a body height greater than 2 m, and a leg length difference greater than 2 cm; (9) osteoporosis; and (10) unstable fractures in the lower extremity or decubitus ulcers on the back or lower extremities. Interventions Explanation for the choice of comparators {6b} Clinical outcomes with neurorehabilitation robots are promising. Robot-assisted gait training improves neuroplasticity, which helps injured nerves recover through repetitive training and stimulation. Second, this training can increase a patient’s muscle strength, stability, walking efficiency, and safety. Electrodes on the skin stimulate spinal circuitries via electrical current in transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), a noninvasive neuromodulation method. This technology may help us understand spinal interneuronal activity and improve rehabilitation for neurological illnesses, including spinal cord injury. The gold standard for SCI rehabilitation is repetitive motor activity, commonly employed in clinics to help patients recover. Exercise after SCI appears to excite the neural system enough to activate undamaged spinal pathways and residual supraspinal inputs [ – ]. Intervention description {11a} The training program for both groups was constructed using the study intervention description from the TIDieR template. Specific information can be found in Additional File 2: Table S2. Each group was undergoing training consisting of 30 30-min sessions per week for 8 weeks. A single instructor with a physical therapy background oversees each training session. The ratio of instructors to participants was 1:1. The training sessions were conducted exclusively in a designated rehabilitation room within the hospital premises. The training sessions for the two groups are scheduled at separate times of the day to ensure that participants are not subjected to additional interventions. Throughout the workout, the participants were closely observed and supervised to ensure their safety and prevent any falls or injuries associated with falling. <italic toggle="yes">Robot-assisted gait training (RAGT)</italic> + <italic toggle="yes">transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS)</italic> The patient received 40 sessions, 5 sessions per week for 8 weeks, of 30 min (Novo Skeleton AVIC Trands Robot Xi'an Co., Ltd., China), and 20 min of tSCS was applied at the beginning of each session. During Novo Skeleton training, the patient fits with a harness and unloads 50% of his body weight. The parameters are adjusted according to the physical characteristics of the patient. The training speed varies between 1.0 and 1.5 km/h, being slow at the beginning of the session and progressively increasing while maintaining gait quality. tSCS was delivered via self-adhesive body surface electrodes for physical therapy BC4060R (pin type); the cathode electrode (4 cm × 6 cm) was placed over (not on the bone but specifically over the soft tissue parallel to the spine) the T11–T12 intervertebral space, and two interconnected reference electrodes (anode) (4 cm × 6 cm) were placed symmetrically at both sides of the umbilicus. A biphasic square current was applied via an electro-stimulator (Xiangyu Electrode Sheet Model 2.0 aperture (TENS), Xiangyu Medical China) with a frequency of 30 Hz and a pulse duration of 1 ms. The stimulation intensity was used at the maximum intensity the patient tolerates during walking because it enhances muscle activation. During volitional exercise, robot-assisted gait training and maximum intensity of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation can significantly increase functional ambulation and independence. For those with spinal cord injuries (SCI), high-intensity electrical stimulation can be quite helpful when it comes to volitional exercises. A pulse that lasts at least 200 µs, with a frequency of 20–60 Hz and an amplitude of up to 300 mA, is recommended because it can help induce powerful muscular contractions and enhance functional mobility. Denervated muscles, which may need up to 100 times more energy to contract, respond best to higher intensities. Criteria for discontinuing or modifying allocated interventions {11b} Participants will be terminated from the trial if they exhibit irreversible exercise-related adverse events, including nausea, dizziness, disorientation, postural instability, and fatigue, even if the trial is exceedingly secure. Strategies to improve adherence to interventions {11c} To optimize instruction compliance, we implement the following strategies: A rigorous training plan was established for each subject every week during the 40-day training period, and the participants’ current circumstances were adjusting the schedule. The feedback and endurance of the participants were closely monitored during the training process. The intervention’s impact on the subjects during training was assessed daily. The decision of patients to withdraw from the study was facilitated. Relevant concomitant care permitted or prohibited during the trial {11d} There are no restrictions regarding concomitant care during the trial. Firstly, no concomitant care participants have been enrolled in the trial due to prior exclusions. There are currently no participants receiving concomitant care. Consequently, there have been no reported complications related to concomitant care. Secondly, concomitant care is not expressly prohibited throughout the trial. However, it is essential to consider the possible interactions and effects that other drugs or treatments may have on the primary and secondary endpoints of the research. We have put the following strategies into practice to lessen any possible confusing factors: Informed consent Participants were asked to disclose any new drugs or treatments they plan to start during the trial, and they were fully educated about the possible risks and benefits of concurrent care. Data collection Including dosage, duration, and reasons for use, we gathered comprehensive information on all concurrent drugs and treatments. Statistical analysis To identify any confounding effects, our statistical analysis plan incorporated techniques to evaluate the possible influence of concurrent care on the study’s outcomes. Through meticulous evaluation and resolution of these variables, our goal is to guarantee the experiment’s validity and the dependability of the results. Provisions for posttrial care {30} N/A. The current study design does not consider ancillary or posttrial care provisions. Additionally, participants will not be harmed by participating in the trial; thus, remuneration for their time is not expected (Tables and ). Outcomes {12} We measured all outcomes twice, once before and once after the 8 weeks of training (Table ), except demographic data. Primary outcomes Berg Balance Scale (BBS) The BBS is a scale of 14 items that measure balance and the likelihood of falling by direct observation. The items are evaluated using a range from 0 to 4, where a score of 0 indicates an inability to complete the assignment and a score of 4 signifies the successful completion of individual tasks. The calculation results in a total score of 56 possible points. The 0–20, 21–40, and 41–56 ratings signify balance impairment, acceptability, and sound, respectively. The BBS has demonstrated exceptional consistency among different raters and within the same rater, with reliability coefficients of 0.99 (95% CI, 0.97–1.00) and perfect agreement with concurrent measures, with a validity coefficient of 1.00 (95% CI, 1.00–1.00) in individuals with incomplete spinal cord damage [ ]. The timer starts counting down from the moment the examiner says “Go,” signaling the start of the test. Afterwards, they get up from their seats, walk 3 m, turn around, return to their seats, and then put themselves back down. The amount of time needed to finish the test determines the score [ ]. Should physical help be needed for walking, this should be done at either the preferred walking speed or the fastest speed achievable. Documentation should include the speed tested (preferred vs. fast) to collect three trials and calculate the average of the three trials. In those with SCI, the 10MWT has shown excellent concept validity (TUG: r = 0.89; 6mWT: r = 0.95) and exceptional test–retest reliability (ICC = 0.983) [ ]. Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury (WISCI II) scale The Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury (WISCI) is a scale used to assess the functional capacity of individuals with SCI regarding their ability to walk. It measures the degree of improvement in ambulation by evaluating the level of physical help, braces, or gadgets needed to walk 10 m. The WISCI II is the latest version. Participants are methodically advanced through a recognized sequence of capacity levels, utilizing gadgets and personal support until they reach their maximum walking ability. The WISCI II categories’ levels are based on the extent of underlying impairment rather than the requirement for physical support, walking aids, or braces. The reliability of repeated WISCI-II scores was high, as measured by intra-rater and inter-rater assessments. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for intra-rater reliability was 0.98, with a confidence interval (CI) of 0.95–0.99. The ICC for inter-rater reliability was 0.97, with a CI of 0.96–0.99 [ ]. Intramuscular electromyography (iEMG) An electrically evoked potential instrument NDI-096-C1 (Suzhou Haishen Medical Equipment Co., Ltd., China) acquired EMG signals at 10,240 Hz and bandpass filters between 100 and 4400 Hz. The intramuscular needle electrode was 0.11 mm in diameter, and a 0.002 m 2 recording area was used for disposable EN-C40 (Suzhou Haishen Medical Equipment Co., Ltd, China). These electrodes were installed with a 0.45-G needle. The fine wires were placed in muscle bellies with a 0.45-gauge hypodermic needle. Before the electrodes were inserted, chlorhexidine was used to clean the area. The electrode’s end connection was fixed after insertion, preventing tugging. The bilateral vastus lateralis (VL), bicep femoris (BF), tibialis anterior (TA), and gastrocnemius medialis capture iEMG activity. Roller bandages are placed on each volunteer’s leg to gather the system’s wire, allowing mobility and eliminating physical interference and noise. Ten ankle flexions and extensions followed 10 knee flexions and extensions. Due to their invasiveness, internal EMG electrodes are rarely utilized. This approach evaluates deep and small cross sections of muscles. Intramuscular EMG is better than surface EMG because it can detect little interference in static and dynamic muscle EMG signals. Every electrode provides a local muscle activity image [ ]. American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale According to the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI), the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS) is the main instrument used in the evaluation of neurological outcomes following spinal cord injury (SCI) [ ]. An instrument that rates motor and sensory ability numerically and provides an alphabetical grade (A–E) to indicate the degree of disability below the level of injury [ ]. The sensory examination tests 28 dermatomes bilaterally for light touch (usually a piece of cotton) and pinprick (usually a clean safety pin). Every examination component is noted for every dermatome and laterality. The absence of sensation is indicated by a score of 0; impaired or changed sensation is indicated by a score of 1, and normal sensation is indicated by a score of 2. With 28 dermatomes, each with 2/2 points for mild touch and 2/2 points for pinprick, a normal unilateral sensory evaluation yields 112 total points. A total normal sensory assessment is a bilateral score of 224. Technically, the inability to differentiate pinprick sensation from mild touch is evaluated as 0 [ ]. Sample size {14} The sample size was calculated via the OpenEpi tool via balance as an outcome measure from the study “Effect of Robotic-assisted Gait Training on Functional and Psychological Improvement in Patients with Incomplete Spinal Cord Injury” [ ]. The level of significance (Z1-α/2) is set at 95%, with an expected mean change in the control group (µ1) of 12.9 and the experimental group (µ2) of 14.3. The anticipated standard deviation for the control group (δ1) is 0.2, whereas for the experimental group (δ2), it is 1.4. The study is powered at 80% (Z1-β) to detect a significant difference between the groups. The initial expected sample size is 18, and after accounting for a 10% dropout rate, the sample size is adjusted to 20. Consequently, the sample size for Group A (control) is 13, and that for Group B (experimental) is 7. The explanation or source for the estimated effect sizes or deviations in the power calculation was provided by referencing the study titled “Effect of Robotic-assisted Gait Training on Functional and Psychological Improvement in Patients with Incomplete Spinal Cord Injury.” The expected mean changes (1.9 for the control group and 14.3 for the experimental group) and the anticipated standard deviations (0.2 for the control group and 1.4 for the experimental group) were derived from this study. This source provides the basis for these estimates, ensuring the power calculation is grounded in empirical data relevant to the research context. The calculation also incorporates a 10% dropout rate adjustment to account for potential participant attrition, further refining the sample size estimates to ensure the study’s validity and reliability. The control group method and efficacy are already mature and effective methods in our hospital. In this experiment, it was only once again proven to be a stable therapy, and the results were also stable, without the need for more cases, which is 1/2 of the experimental group. Additionally, performing nonparametric tests is advantageous with small samples because they require fewer assumptions, are robust to outliers, and offer more straightforward, reliable results. Data collection and management Plans for assessment and collection of outcomes {18a} To ensure the quality of the research, we will conduct a thorough evaluation of the recruited doctors, rehabilitation therapists, assessors, and pertinent equipment prior to the commencement of the study. The following specific steps are taken: The experimental procedure was performed entirely by the recruited doctors. The therapists received instructions on the proper conduct of the training program and the management of potential adverse events that may arise during training. The assessors received training in the suitable handling and processing of outcome indicators. The lower limb rehabilitation robot (Novoskeleton AVIC Trands Robot, electromyography/evoked potential instrument NDI-096-C1) and electro-stimulator (Xiangyu Electrode Sheet Model 2.0 aperture (TENS)) were debugged to achieve the optimal running state of the equipment. Plans to promote participant retention and complete follow-up {18b} The subsequent evaluation was conducted 8 weeks after completing the training program. The participants were contacted via telephone and invited to the hospital to undergo the assessment. Data management {19} The hospital’s safety supervision committee oversees the project, which is tasked with evaluating experimental design, scientific rigor, participant safety, adherence to medical ethics, and proper data management. Strict measures were implemented to safeguard the privacy rights of each participant. Initial data and outcome indicators were securely stored in a highly protected database, and anonymization procedures were rigorously followed to ensure the safety and confidentiality of all participants. Confidentiality {27} Confidentiality rules were strictly followed during the experiment to gather, distribute, and safeguard personal information of potential and enrolled participants. Before starting the study, each participant provided informed consent, including a detailed explanation of the study’s aim, procedures, and potential hazards. The consent was obtained via a particular protocol code. Throughout the study, all the gathered data undergo confidentiality and was securely stored, with access limited exclusively to authorized individuals responsible for data analysis and trial supervision. Once the trial ended, personal information was protected, and any remaining identifiable data (specific protocol code) was securely stored for the necessary retention period. This was done in accordance with institutional and regulatory guidelines that ensure confidentiality and data protection. Groups were well matched at baseline on sex and all clinical and neurophysiological measures (all p ≥ 0.096), supporting unbiased estimation of treatment effects. Across 8 weeks, both arms improved substantially; however, improvement trajectories consistently favored RAGT + tSCS. Significant time × group interactions were observed for the Berg Balance Scale (BBS; F = 42.465, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.702), Timed Up and Go (TUG; F = 97.500, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.844), WISCI-II ( F = 8.528, p = 0.009, partial η 2 = 0.321), ASIA motor ( F = 56.639, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.759), and three of four intramuscular EMG (iEMG) targets: vastus lateralis, tibialis anterior, and gastrocnemius medialis (all p < 0.001; partial η 2 = 0.880, 0.859, 0.924, respectively). Post-intervention contrasts underscored clinically meaningful advantages: adjusted BBS was higher by + 7.67 points (95% CI, 5.14–10.19; partial η 2 = 0.708); TUG was faster by − 10.91 s, WISCI-II by + 1.26 points, and ASIA motor by + 7.93 points; and iEMG amplitudes were substantially larger in agonists critical for stance and foot-clearance (e.g., tibialis anterior + 217.7 µV). The 10-m walk test (10MWT) increased similarly in both groups (RAGT + tSCS + 0.092 m/s vs CPT + tSCS + 0.086 m/s, between-group p = 0.885), a pattern addressed below. How our findings fit with and extend current evidence Our result pattern mirrors high-quality syntheses of randomized trials comparing robotic exoskeleton gait training (REGT) with conventional therapy. A 2025 meta-analysis of 15 RCTs ( n = 579) found that, on average, REGT does not outperform conventional therapy for walking speed (10MWT weighted mean difference [WMD] − 0.03 m/s, p = 0.08) or 6-min walk distance (6MWT WMD − 1.83 m, p = 0.78) while consistently improving TUG (WMD 6.62 s, p = 0.04), WISCI-II (WMD 2.17, p = 0.0001), and lower-extremity motor scores (LEMS WMD 1.33, p = 0.0005) [ ]. Device family matters: in subgroup analyses, Lokomat improved WISCI-II (WMD 2.05, p = 0.005) and LEMS (WMD 1.22, p = 0.002), while wearable exoskeletons improved WISCI-II (WMD 2.75, p = 0.0005) but not LEMS (WMD 2.88, p = 0.06) [ , ]. Timing also moderates effects: within ≤ 6-month post-injury, REGT and conventional therapy are roughly equivalent for speed/distance, whereas beyond 6 months conventional therapy may hold an advantage for speed [ ]. These patterns, stronger effects on dynamic balance, ambulation complexity, and motor scores than on short-distance speed, map closely onto our between-group differences (BBS, TUG, WISCI-II, ASIA motor) and the non-separation on 10MWT at 8 weeks. Crucially, convergent evidence indicates that adding tSCS to standardized robotic stepping can unlock advantages that are not always seen with RAGT alone, particularly after a consolidation interval. In a double-blind, sham-controlled RCT pairing tSCS with a fixed Lokomat program ( n = 27), no between-group differences were evident immediately poststimulation block for primary outcomes; however, superiority of active tSCS emerged at 1-month follow-up for LEMS (Δ 3.3 points, p = 0.033), 10MWT (faster by 0.037 m/s, p = 0.030), TUG (− 4.7 s, p = 0.030), and WISCI-II (+ 3.4 points, p = 0.023). The absence of a group interaction for biceps femoris is coherent with (i) the specific task demands emphasized by our progression and (ii) measurement selectivity: by using iEMG, which offers higher spatial specificity and signal-to-noise than surface EMG in neurological cohorts, we increase confidence that the observed changes reflect true neural recruitment rather than cross-talk or adiposity-related filtering [ , ]. Independent neurophysiology from the sham-controlled RCT, greater tibialis-anterior MEP amplitude with active tSCS, converges with our iEMG pattern and further supports a corticospinal/spinal priming mechanism that consolidates with subsequent conventional sessions [ , ]. First, treadmill-based RAGT emphasizes kinematic guidance, loading, and postural control, components that translate more directly to TUG/WISCI-II than to short distance, overground peak velocity unless explicit speed-targeted overground progression is incorporated [ , ]. Second, speed is notably sensitive to post-injury timing and dose; pooled RCT evidence indicates little to no advantage of REGT over conventional care for speed in the subacute window, with conventional care sometimes outperforming REGT > 6 months after injury [ , ]. Third, the double-blind tSCS + Lokomat RCT demonstrates that speed gains can lag, emerging after a month of continued practice (Δ 0.037 m/s) [ , ]. Finally, at the very low baseline velocities in our cohort (~ 0.23–0.24 m/s), absolute changes that are clinically meaningful may remain below between-group detectability in modest samples and with heterogeneous assistive-device use, one reason meta-analyses urge reporting of effect sizes and responder analyses, not just p -values [ , ]. Body-weight support (BWS) requirements correlated strongly and negatively with assignment at session 1 ( r = − 0.886, p < 0.001) and session 20 ( r = − 0.867, p < 0.001), indicating more aggressive BWS reduction in the robotic arm, a plausible treatment mediator rather than a confound, because lowering support is intrinsic to the therapeutic mechanism that tSCS may help tolerate by increasing network excitability. Anthropometrics and time since injury showed expected collinearities (e.g., age with weight and height) but did not differ by group, reducing the likelihood of systematic confounding. These observations align with meta-analytic notes that dose heterogeneity (30–90 min per session, 4–8 weeks total) and device-specific progression strategies contribute to between-study dispersion of effect sizes [ , ]. Across RAGT trials and syntheses, REGT is likewise framed as safe and feasible in both inpatient and outpatient settings, with favorable cardiovascular adaptations reported over extended programs. Of note, for clinical translation, randomized evidence suggests respiratory benefits with REGT (FEV1 WMD + 0.60 L, p = 0.03), even though effects on FVC and PEF are less consistent (two RCTs, n = 34) [ , ]. These secondary system outcomes, together with potential improvements in orthostatic tolerance and aerobic capacity reported in contemporary reviews, support earlier mobilization and may compound the functional gains of neuromodulation-augmented stepping [ , , ]. Methodological work shows that in randomized pre- and post-designs, ANCOVA (post adjusted for baseline) provides greater power and precision than change scores or multiple t -tests by reducing residual variance and addressing residual baseline differences [ – ]. Limitations include modest sample size (particularly for velocity outcomes with floor effects), the absence of a post-block follow-up (precluding direct observation of delayed superiority for speed), and device or contextual specificity (treadmill-based RAGT with specific progression heuristics), which may limit generalizability across the broader RAGT ecosystem [ , ]. As emphasized by recent syntheses, heterogeneity in dose, device, chronicity, and inclusion of some AIS-A participants can blunt pooled speed effects and warrant careful reporting of effect sizes, precision, and responders alongside null hypothesis tests [ , ]. These constraints also justify the use of multivariate and repeated-measures models rather than the initially planned t -tests, providing a more efficient and statistically stable framework that allowed correlated endpoints to be analyzed jointly, controlled type 1 error, and preserved power despite the limited sample size and inter-outcome covariance [ , ]. Clinical implications and future directions For people with incomplete SCI, these results support integrating tSCS during high-dose robotic stepping to accelerate gains in balance, complex mobility, ambulation level, and motor index, domains with clear relevance toward safety, transfers, turning, and discharge independence. To realize durable advantages in speed, programs should add explicit, overground, speed-targeted progression and schedule follow-up assessments to capture neuromodulation-enabled consolidation. Future trials should (i) standardize BWS and speed-progression algorithms, (ii) compare device families head-to-head under identical neuromodulation, (iii) leverage biomarkers (baseline corticospinal excitability, iEMG motor-unit metrics) to profile responders, and (iv) extend observation windows beyond the intervention block to adjudicate the priming-and-consolidation hypothesis more directly [ , , , , ]. Given preliminary signals for cardiorespiratory benefits, incorporating spirometry and ambulatory hemodynamics could clarify secondary health impacts that matter for real-world participation [ , , ]. Conclusions RAGT paired with tSCS produced larger improvements than CPT + tSCS in balance (BBS), functional mobility (TUG), ambulation level (WISCI-II), ASIA motor, and targeted muscle recruitment (iEMG), with parallel changes in short-distance walking speed at 8 weeks. Read against current evidence, the data support a model in which tSCS gates spinal networks during task-specific stepping to amplify the domains RAGT already tends to improve, while speed differentials are expected to emerge with consolidation and speed-focused overground practice. This neuromodulation-augmented approach is biologically plausible, clinically feasible, and aligned with evolving RCT syntheses; it merits scaled testing with device-specific optimization, longer follow-up, and responder-oriented design. chunks.content: 1. Introduction Our understanding of the intricacies and pathways underlying the pathophysiology of SCI has evolved significantly over the past three decades. This has led to several paradigm shifts concerning the management of SCI. Specifically, the importance of mitigating secondary injury mechanisms following the initial physical trauma has been highlighted by several landmark studies [ , , ]. Several candidate strategies have been studied that target various components of this chemical and molecular injury cascade [ , ]. Despite these advances, the neurological prognosis for most SCI patients remains poor. Regaining lost neurologic function, particularly quadriparesis or quadriplegia in cases of cervical SCI and paraparesis or paraplegia in cases of thoracolumbar SCI, continues to be a significant challenge. The factors that impede regeneration after SCI include axonal degeneration, inhibitory factors in the post-injury micro-environment, particularly the chronic astroglial scar, and loss of neuronal and oligodendroglial populations [ ]. From a public health perspective, neurotrauma involving the brain and spine has been shown to be the leading cause of disability around the world [ ]. Optimizing treatment outcomes can be aided by customizing management to identify persons living with SCI who have the highest potential to gain from neuroprotective and/or neuroregenerative approaches [ ]. In the current review, the authors first examine the difficulties associated with conducting research on SCI, including the challenges when assessing the severity of SCI as well as the limitations of traditional statistics when evaluating treatment efficacy. The authors then explore advances in surgical management and promising recent translational advances for SCI. 2. Challenges in SCI Research SCI represents a complex and heterogenous clinical entity characterized by diverse presentations and outcomes. The interplay of factors such as the injury level, severity, and associated comorbidities contributes to the wide variability observed among SCI patients, impacting their motor, sensory, psychological and social outcomes. The evolving landscape of SCI’s epidemiology reflects its inherent heterogeneity. While significant progress in public health efforts has reduced the incidence of SCIs from motor vehicular collisions (MVCs), sports and occupational trauma in high-income countries, a notable increase in SCI cases among the elderly, particularly due to falls, has been observed. A study by Aarabi et al. demonstrated that across a 17-year span, the average age and proportion of SCI cases resulting from falls increased significantly, while those arising from MVCs and sports-related injuries declined [ ]. This demographic shift is further corroborated by a US-based study reporting the rising mean age of SCI patients from 40 years in 1993 to 50 years in 2012 [ ]. Projections suggest that the majority of traumatic SCI patients will exceed 70 years of age by the year 2032 [ ]. The complexity of SCI is likewise evident in the multitude of scales employed to assess and grade SCI patients across various domains. Such complexity demands innovative solutions to represent the clinical profiles and outcomes of these patients. Relying solely on a traditional singular scale such as the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS) may be restrictive, given the breadth of factors influencing SCI outcomes. Embracing adaptive clinical trial designs and multiparametric outcome representation enables researchers to capture the nuanced nature of SCI presentation and treatment responses [ ]. Trajectory modeling offers a dynamic framework for analyzing patient outcomes over time, revealing unique clinical profiles and prognostic indicators. This approach has revealed targeted clinical relationships between variables and patient outcomes among those with incomplete and complete SCI. Additionally, machine-learning algorithms, including supervised- and unsupervised-learning techniques, provide powerful tools for extracting meaningful insights from complex SCI datasets [ ]. By leveraging large-scale data repositories and advanced computational methods, machine leaning can facilitate personalized risk stratification and treatment allocation in SCI management. These innovative methodologies both enhance the scientific rigor of research as well as hold promise for translating research findings into meaningful improvements in SCI care and outcomes. 3. Hemodynamic Management In addition to surgical decompression, controlling the mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) offers clinicians an opportunity to optimize recovery and prevent further ischemic damage to the spinal cord after injury. Patients are closely monitored for respiratory insufficiency, cardiac dysfunction, and systemic hypotension post-injury [ ]. Hypovolemia from concurrent bleeding and neurogenic shock increases the risk of systemic hypotension in SCI patients, which further aggravates secondary injury to the spinal cord. Reduced MAP has been suggested to have a major impact on the spinal cord through alterations in the oxygen supply to susceptible tissue, a decrease in spinal cord perfusion, and a worsening of secondary damage. The damaged spinal cord’s compromised vascular responsiveness and loss of autoregulation renders it especially vulnerable to systemic hypotension. According to Ryken et al., volume expansion and deliberate blood pressure increases were believed to enhance the neurological outcomes as well as lower mortality and morbidity in patients with SCI [ ]. In order to synthesize the effects of goal-directed interventions aimed at optimizing spinal cord perfusion on neurological recovery and adverse events, as well as the effects of monitoring techniques, perfusion ranges, pharmacological therapies, and treatment duration, Evaniew et al. (2020) conducted a high-quality systematic review of the current evidence base [ ]. Pertinent interventional and observational research, both prospective and retrospective, was included in this study. The analysis highlighted several limitations of previous systematic reviews, specifically that none evaluated the possibility of bias in the included studies or employed the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) methodology to appraise the quality of the available evidence. Moreover, no other evaluations have examined the effects on neurological outcomes of combined spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) and MAP. This systematic review also noted that across studies, it remained unclear how increasing MAP would affect neurological recovery [ ]. Several included studies showed that (i) the motor scores did not differ between patients who received vasopressors and those who did not, and (ii) the MAP decreases were not linked to changes in the ASIA motor scores [ , ]. While MAP support was found to be effective in other included investigations, these studies had lower sample sizes and MINORS (Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies) scores, which suggests a higher risk of bias [ ]. Additionally, there are little data to support the hypothesis that vasopressor support of MAP is linked to a higher incidence of arrhythmias, cardiac damage, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome [ ]. The approach to hemodynamic care for acute SCI must take all of these aspects into account. While the use of SCPP has been shown to produce better neurological outcomes as measured by the AIS [ ], using intradural catheters to evaluate SCPP is an invasive monitoring method that can increase the risk of meningitis or CSF leak [ ]. Reviewing the strength of the evidence for the possible benefits of elevating MAP or SCPP, weighing the potential risks associated with each strategy, and assessing the viability and cost-effectiveness of these treatments are all crucial when establishing recommendations. Expansile Duraplasty The first recommendation for the use of expansile duraplasty was made by Werndle et al. [ ], in connection with monitoring spinal cord perfusion after decompression to check for SCI. Following injury, there is increased edema and swelling of the spinal cord parenchyma, causing it to compress against the surrounding dura. This causes an abrupt and localized rise in intraspinal pressure (ISP), ultimately inhibiting autoregulation. Impaired autoregulation is associated with increased SCPP (e.g., hyperperfusion) and decreased SCPP (e.g., hypoperfusion), which may result in further SCI akin to intracranial dynamics. Consequently, it has been suggested in some reports to utilize a posterior midline dural incision made longitudinally for duraplasty purposes after bone decompression. While this practice may enhance the ISP as well as SCPP and provide additional decompression to the spinal cord, its benefits must be weighed against other potential risks, including infection and CSF leak [ ]. A prospective, phase III, multicenter randomized controlled trial is currently underway to investigate if, among acutely injured cervical SCI patients, the addition of dural decompression in combination with bony decompression will improve muscle strength at 6 months using the AIS motor score as the primary outcome. The DISCUS (Duraplasty for Injured Cervical Spinal Cord with Uncontrolled Swelling) study ( NCT04936620 ) is currently recruiting patients and is estimated to be completed in 2026 [ ]. 3.5. Therapeutic Hypothermia Therapeutic hypothermia has been recommended as a supplement to the conventional care of SCI due to its neuroprotective properties. It is thought to reduce bleeding, edema, and pressure while interrupting glutamate excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Pre-clinical and early clinical trials investigating the use of therapeutic hypothermia for SCI suggest it may have a role as a neuroprotective strategy. Following an injury, therapeutic hypothermia can be used locally or systemically through endovascular, extradural, or intradural methods. Based on data from human trials, Shin et al. conducted a recent meta-analysis and found that, while systemic hypothermia was not statistically significant, it was preferable to local hypothermia in terms of the improved neurological outcomes. Further research is required on the means of inducing therapeutic hypothermia and determining the optimal temperature target. While physical techniques like cooling fluid have been most commonly examined for SCI and other conditions, including stroke, pharmacological techniques to produce therapeutic hypothermia are a novel area of investigation. Pharmacological Advances A key element of the pathophysiology of SCI involves neurodegeneration, which is characterized by progressive loss of neurons and synapses. Numerous chemical and molecular events contribute to degeneration, including oxidative stress, apoptosis, inflammation, and excitotoxicity [ ]. Since neurons have limited capacity to regenerate, neuronal damage is frequently irreparable and irreversible [ ]. Significant work has been conducted to study candidate pharmacological agents with the potential to enhance repair and regeneration after SCI. The possibility of using currently available medications with neuroprotective or pro-regenerative capabilities makes “drug repurposing” a very attractive prospect in the context of SCI. Since these medications have already been evaluated and approved for other medical disorders, repurposing them can save significant capital and time. The utilization of drug repurposing holds promise in expeditiously identifying pharmaceuticals suitable for clinical trials, thereby facilitating the identification of agents that effectively enhance outcomes for individuals with SCI [ ]. In the following section, we will discuss some of the biological and pharmacological agents currently being evaluated in preclinical and clinical trials for SCI ( ). 4.1.1. Riluzole Riluzole, a benzothiazole anticonvulsant, has been shown to have neuroprotective properties, likely due to its mechanism of blocking sodium channels, which in turn helps to reduce excitotoxic injury [ , , ]. In a rodent cervical spine hemisection model, Satkunendrarah et al. showed that riluzole treatment increased the preservation of glutamatergic synapses and motor neurons caudal to the lesion site, resulting in improved locomotor and respiratory function [ ]. Riluzole has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials as a potential therapy for SCI. Variable levels of peak plasma concentration were identified in a phase I trial ( NCT00876889 ) evaluating the safety and pharmacokinetics of riluzole in acute traumatic SCI. No major side effects were observed; however, some patients did experience mild-to-moderate elevations in liver enzymes. Patients in the riluzole group were reported to demonstrate greater improvements in the average motor score [ , , , , , , , ]. The Riluzole in Spinal Cord Injury Study (RISCIS), a subsequent phase IIB/III clinical trial, was discontinued because of enrollment issues during the COVID-19 pandemic. The trial’s goal was to assess improvements in the motor scores of the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI). Due to insufficient power secondary to early termination, the authors were unable to achieve the pre-set endpoint to evaluate efficacy. However, all cervical SCI patient subgroups (AIS grades A, B, and C) treated with riluzole demonstrated improvements in functional recovery, which were part of the preplanned secondary analyses. 4.1.2. Precision Medicine For many years, efforts have been made in SCI research to improve the capacity to reliably predict neurological and functional outcomes in SCI patients. Imaging, serum, and CSF biomarkers have been examined as potential modalities to predict the neurological outcomes and the severity of neural injury. 4.2.1. Imaging Biomarkers Accurate and unbiased neuroimaging measurements may have the potential to predict pathophysiological alterations in the spinal cord and explain neurological heterogeneity after injury. Determining imaging biomarkers that correlate with neurological function and recovery may aid in prediction and patient stratification. Martin et al. recently described a radiographic white matter injury biomarker that corresponds with focal motor and sensory abnormalities. Specifically, it measures the signal intensity of white to gray matter on T2*-weighted imaging [ ]. In addition, the neurological deficits of patients at baseline have been shown to have some associations with the IMLL, maximum spinal cord compression (MSCC), and maximum canal compromise (MCC) [ , ]. Patients with sensorimotor complete SCI have been shown to have more extensive acute lesion lengths, MSCCs, and MCCs, with the latter being correlated with baseline AIS grades. Similarly, baseline motor scores are associated with more prominent MSCC and MCC [ , ]. CSF Biomarkers The levels of specific molecules have been found to be elevated in the CSF following traumatic brain injury (TBI) and SCI [ , ]. Thus, molecular analysis of CSF from SCI patients has the potential to uncover biomarkers of clinical relevance that may help diagnose, assess severity, and predict outcomes. The clinical feasibility of this approach, however, remains challenging as CSF is not routinely collected after SCI [ ]. Furthermore, obtaining CSF through a lumbar puncture is invasive and may have associated risks [ , ]. In a recent study consisting of 50 SCI patients, called the CAMPER (Canadian Multicentre CSF Monitoring and Biomarker Study) study, there was a significant difference in the CSF levels of GFAP, tau, IL-6, and S100b, at 24 h post-injury between ASIA A, B and C patients ( NCT01279811 ) [ ]. Furthermore, the CSF levels of these molecules were found to be associated with ASIA motor score improvement, particularly for patients with cervical SCI. In comparison to MRI-based biomarkers, CSF biomarkers may be more likely to identify distinct damage predictors and have a superior ability to predict neurological recovery [ ]. Several other inflammatory mediators have been studied in CSF samples from patients with SCI. Studies have reported the CSF of SCI patients to contain higher levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-8, IL-16, TNF), chemokines (e.g., C-X-C motif chemokine (CXCL)-10, neutrophil attractant protein (NAP)-2, monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP)-1), and growth factors (e.g., nerve growth factor (NGF)) [ , , , ] The clinical utility of these agents requires further investigation. 4.2.3. Serological and Genetic Biomarkers While CSF biomarkers may provide valuable information for SCI prediction or patient stratification, its clinical utility is hindered by the invasive nature of sample collection. As such, there is great appeal in studying serological or blood-based biomarkers. In clinical studies, higher concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, colony stimulating factor-1, IL-2, IL-2R, IL-3, IL-6, IL 9, IL-16, IL-18) were present in the serum of SCI patients compared to those in the control group [ , , , , , , , , , , , ] Frost et al. (2005) found that 37 individuals with chronic SCI did not have higher levels of TNF or IL-6, in contrast to several earlier investigations [ ]. SCI patients have also been shown to have elevated levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 and the IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), in addition to a pro-inflammatory cytokine profile. In contrast, the levels of several pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, sIL-2Rα, IL-4, IL-5, IL-7, IL-13, IL-17, interferon-γ) and chemokines (macrophage inflammatory protein-1α and MIP-1β and granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulation factor) were significantly lower in acute SCI patients compared to non-SCI patients. In particular, the circulating levels of IL-10 were significantly higher in SCI patients than in non-SCI patients [ ]. 4.3. Regenerative and Cell-Based

Regenerative and Cell-Based Therapies Over the past few decades, cellular transplantation as a regenerative therapy for SCI has attracted a lot of attention. This is due to the fact that cell-based strategies may target several elements of the secondary injury cascade of SCI. For example, cell transplantation can provide trophic support, regulate the inflammatory response, repair damaged neuronal circuits, and regenerate denuded axons. Neural stem cells (NSCs), mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), olfactory ensheathing cells (OECs), and Schwann cells are the most commonly examined cell types ( ) [ , ]. 4.3.1. Neural Stem Cells (NSCs) Due to their tripotent self-renewing capacity, neural stem cells have been shown to improve functional recovery by myelinating denuded axons and encouraging tissue sparing in animal models of SCI [ ]. NSCs significantly improve neurological function in preclinical SCI models, according to a 2016 meta-analysis (pooled SMD = 1.45; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.23–1.67; p < 0.001) [ ]. Patients with thoracic AIS grades A–C and cervical AIS grades B or C SCI underwent intramedullary injections of human fetal CNS human stem cells (HuCNS-SC) as part of a phase II trial conducted by StemCells Inc. While positive trends toward the Upper Extremity Motor Score (UEMS) and Graded Redefined Assessment of Strength, Sensibility, and Prehension (GRASSP) motor gains were shown in the interim analysis of patients who were transplanted with HuCNS-SCs, the magnitude of the improvement was below the clinical efficacy threshold that the sponsor had set in order to support further development. Therefore, the trial was terminated early [ ]. Stem cell transplantation may work synergistically with other therapies. For instance, transplantation of NSCs in combination with the delivery of chondroitinase ABC (ChABC), used to degrade the glial scar, was shown to improve recovery in animal models of SCI [ ] ( ). 4.3.2. Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) Over the past few years, there has been increasing interest in bone marrow-derived stem cells as a possible therapeutic agent for a variety of illnesses. These cells have lower immunogenicity when allografted, and they release cytokines as well as exosomes that reduce inflammation [ ]. In SCI, mesenchymal stem cells are thought to work by first migrating into the injured cord and then changing phenotypically to become neural cell phenotypes that allow factors promoting repair to be expressed rather than replacing damaged cells [ ]. Multipotent MSCs can be extracted from readily accessible tissue, including fat, bone marrow, and skeletal muscle [ ]. They also proliferate quickly, show little immunoreactivity upon allogenic transplantation, and remain alive after being cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen or at −80 °C [ , , ]. This has prompted their translation into a number of areas, including arthritis [ ], multiple sclerosis [ ], and sepsis [ ]. Through neurotrophic signaling and immunomodulation, MSCs have been demonstrated to greatly improve tissue sparing and stimulate angiogenesis in SCI [ , ]. Additionally, studies have suggested that MSCs injected directly into the spinal cord can control macrophage activity and encourage tissue sparing [ , ]. There are several active clinical trials evaluating the safety, efficacy, and dosage of MSCs produced from adipocytes. A phase I study of 1 × 10 8 autologous adipose-derived MSCs administered intrathecally to patients with AIS grade A/B/C 2 weeks to 1 year after injury is being carried out at the Mayo Clinic (N = 10; clinicaltrials.gov identifier NCT03308565 ). The investigation is scheduled to be finished in June 2024 [ ]. The effectiveness of injecting bone marrow-derived stem cells above, inside, and into the injury cavity, as well as the subdural space, was studied in a phase 3 experiment. UC-MSCs are typically extracted from cord tissue, cord blood, or Wharton’s jelly, a gelatinous material found in the cord. Since umbilical cord tissue is easily obtained and often discarded, MSCs derived from it have been shown to be less susceptible to rejection, as indicated by a decreased risk of graft-versus-host disease [ ]. The quantity of MSCs found in cord blood or placental tissues is lower than in adult sources, but they can be easily grown, and the tissue can be frozen and used for isolation at a later time [ ]. It has also been demonstrated that MSCs obtained from the umbilical cord possess immunomodulatory qualities [ ]. In a study by Moinuddin et al., the authors performed a T9 contusion and then randomized 12 female Sprague Dawley rats to either a control or rat UC-MSC group. By 14 weeks after their injuries, animals receiving rUC-MSC treatment demonstrated early and persistent motor recovery [ ]. In order to evaluate allogeneic UC-derived MSCs for subacute and chronic SCI, a number of recently registered phase I/II trials ( NCT03505034 [ ]; NCT02481440 [ ]; NCT03521323 ) [ ] are currently accepting participants ( ). 4.3.3. Oligodendrocyte Progenitor Cells (OPCs) Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) are another cell source that has been studied in the treatment of SCI, given their potential to develop into myelinating oligodendrocytes. Based on pre-clinical studies, OPCs have been shown to improve motor recovery by reducing the cavitation volume, enhancing the white matter sparing, and increasing oligodendrocyte survival [ ]. In the SCiStar trial, AIS grade A and B patients with subaxial cervical injuries received intramedullary injections of OPCs. The results showed that 95% of patients (21/22) recovered at least one motor level on one side, and 32% (7/22) recovered two or more motor levels on one side [ ] ( ). 4.3.4. Schwann Cells Schwann cells of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) are myelinating cells that express growth-promoting proteins and act as a structural framework to direct developing axons and myelinate regenerating axons [ ]. Immunosuppression is not required for the manufacture of autologous cell transplants, thanks to dependable cell culture techniques. Schwann cells travel with axons throughout the process of neurodevelopment. These cells, together with the basal lamina components they release, form tubular bands during nerve healing. These tubular bands allow axons to either regenerate or contract, depending on whether they are surrounded by the extracellular matrix or the cytoplasm of non-myelinating Schwann cells. The ligands known to be involved in this process of nerve regeneration include the binding of laminin’s RGD peptide to axonal L1-NCAM. Gene expression alterations accompany the myelinating to non-myelinating phenotypic transition in Schwann cells. Schwann cells have the ability to revert to a stable myelinating subtype during nerve regeneration. The sparse integration of Schwann cells with astrocytes and oligodendroglia is one of the drawbacks of transplanting the cells into the central nervous system. A phase 1 clinical trial was conducted recently in the US, which examined the safety of intramedullary transplanted autologous Schwann cells for complete thoracic SCI. The trial included six patients. Each patient’s sural nerve was used to extract cells, which were then preprocessed in vitro to ensure healthy cell proliferation. The cells were transplanted 30–60 days following damage; five million cells were transplanted in two patients, ten million cells in two more patients, and fifteen million cells in the final two patients when the dose was increased to evaluate the dose-dependent safety. Under ultrasound guidance, cells were transferred into the exposed damage epicenter using a stereotactic syringe-positioning device. In terms of safety, there have been no adverse effects associated with nerve harvesting or the transplant surgery. For AIS grade A to B patients, the clinical improvements reported in the study were within the typical range for those with thoracic SCIs. Subclinical improvements in the motor cortical connections were observed in neurophysiological investigations (motor evoked potentials and electromyography), with enhanced activity, particularly below the initial spinal level at which damage was discovered. Through numerous international research efforts, the viability and safety of administering stem cells to the injured spinal cord are described in a systematic review of clinical trials. Nevertheless, the efficacy is still under verification. Research is currently ongoing to determine the best cell type and transplantation technique for lesion bridging and remodeling, lowering immunological rejection, as well as creating stable circuits [ ] ( ). 4.4. Nevertheless, the efficacy is still under verification. Research is currently ongoing to determine the best cell type and transplantation technique for lesion bridging and remodeling, lowering immunological rejection, as well as creating stable circuits [ ] ( ). 4.4. Endogenous Stem Cells In addition to the transplantation of exogenous cells, there is great appeal in harnessing the spinal cord’s own capacity for regeneration. The central canal region of the spinal cord contains a population of ependymal derived neural stem/progenitor cells that may possess stem cell-like properties. While normally quiescent, these cells become activated after SCI and primarily differentiate into astrocytes, with a smaller subset acquiring an oligodendrocytic fate. Several studies have demonstrated that these cells are important in promoting axon regeneration, providing beneficial trophic support and contributing to baseline functional recovery [ , , ]. Current efforts aim to study strategies to further enhance the activation of endogenous ependymal derived neural stem/progenitor cells and direct their fate specification [ , , ] ( ). 4.5. Biomaterials/Scaffolds For targeted and sustained medication delivery, a variety of biomaterial scaffolds have been examined [ ]. These have been shown to promote the development, survival, and plasticity of cells by introducing exogenous stem cells into the injured area as well as providing an environment and scaffold for the regeneration of endogenous circuits [ , ]. When injected into the spinal cord cavity, QL6, a biodegradable peptide, forms nanofiber scaffolds that decrease inflammation, apoptosis, and astrocyte lysis, leading to improvements in behavior as well as electrophysiology [ , ]. In the INSPIRE trial, 19 patients had open surgery to implant the Neuro-Spinal Scaffold 96 h after their injuries. At 24 months, there were no long-term neurological complications, and at 12 months and beyond, favorable AIS conversions were observed [ ] ( ). 4.6. Upregulating Intrinsic Regenerative Potential Reactivating intrinsic growth programs and promoting axon regeneration through the manipulation of neuronal intrinsic factors have been the focus of extensive research recently. Some of the primary intrinsic processes that govern axon regeneration are cytoskeletal dynamics, ion channels, and signaling pathways. We discuss a few advances in these areas here [ ]. Following a mild spinal cord contusion in rats, it has been demonstrated that the microtubule-stabilizing medications Taxol and epothilone B promote microtubule polymerization and reduce fibrotic scarring, thereby inducing axon regeneration and improving function [ ]. Neuronal survival and axon growth are regulated by intracellular signaling pathways, including DLK, JAK/STAT/SOCS3, and mTOR. A growing body of research indicates that adjusting these pathways may improve neuroplasticity and intrinsic growth competence following spinal cord injury [ , , , , ]. Voltage-gated calcium channels’ α2δ2 subunit functions as a developmental switch that limits axon growth and regeneration while favorably controlling synapse formation. Mice with crush SCI showed enhanced regeneration of CST and ascending sensory axons when α2δ2 was pharmacologically blocked with gabapentinoid [ , , ]. 4.7. Neuromodulation and Brain–Spine Interfaces When combined with physical rehabilitation, lumbar spinal cord stimulation (SCS) has improved stepping and ambulation in patients with chronic SCI. After a week of combined therapy, improvements in locomotion have been observed, with lasting improvements in ground walking at the 1-year follow-up [ , ]. In recent years, there has been an increase in the use of brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) to regulate upper extremity function, which includes reaching and gripping. For patients to benefit, it is crucial to bring this technology into a community setting that is closer to their homes. Either soft robotics (SR) or functional electrical stimulation (FES) constitute the technical foundation of the majority of these interactions [ ]. Traditional FES therapy involves teaching patients to voluntarily contract their muscles to perform a predetermined task while surface-level or implanted electrodes from the FES system stimulate the muscles. According to this approach, conscious movements occur simultaneously with peripheral sensations and brain activity brought on by the conscious effort. The FES generates additional afferent input, which enhances practice-induced plasticity in the brain and spinal cord [ , , ]. SR devices use soft actuators, which are frequently back-drivable, and flexible connections to improve comfort and flexibility while adapting to the natural curves of the human body. SR hand-function devices are lightweight and portable, making them easy to use at home for rehabilitation [ , ]. 5. Current research in the area of pharmacological agents, cell-based therapies, endogenous regeneration and electrical stimulation aims to mitigate different components of the secondary injury cascade as well as to enhance damage repair mechanisms.
